metadata.title: Take the Test: Sample Questions from OECD’s PISA Assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD volume is a compilation of publicly released PISA sample questions and scoring information, not an analysis of student microdata. It describes how PISA is administered (randomly selected schools, two-hour test, and a student questionnaire) and how responses are scored using detailed scoring guides, but it does not provide a dataset extract, analytic sample, or any weighting/replicate-weight variables. Because no empirical modeling is conducted here, there is no basis to specify which student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) would be applied. For any secondary analysis using PISA microdata, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights supplied with the dataset to account for the complex survey design and nested sampling (students within schools within countries).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document does not conduct an empirical student-level analysis with a cognitive achievement dependent variable; instead, it presents sample PISA tasks and scoring guidance. As a result, plausible values (PV-based achievement scores) are not generated or modeled, and there is no missing-data handling procedure to report for an ML/statistical estimation step. The only quantitative elements shown are item-level scoring/difficulty descriptions and percentages of students answering correctly across OECD countries for illustrative purposes, not an estimation pipeline requiring PV or missing-data treatment.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No analytic sample is defined because the report does not analyze PISA microdata. It instead presents publicly released PISA reading, mathematics, and science tasks (and their scoring guidance) that were used in PISA 2000/2003/2006 or in developing and trying out the surveys. The report notes that PISA tests 15-year-old students in randomly selected schools and that administration typically covers between 4,500 and 40,000 students per country, but it does not specify any subset selection, exclusions, or task-level completion filters for an empirical dataset.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume explains what PISA assesses and provides publicly released sample questions from the PISA reading, mathematics, and science assessments. It describes the PISA framework as “literacy” (applied ability to use knowledge in real-life contexts), the three-year cycle (2000, 2003, 2006), and the administration procedure (two-hour test in randomly selected schools plus a student questionnaire). It also explains how responses are scored using detailed scoring guides (full/partial/no credit) and how results are reported on proficiency scales (e.g., average 500 with two-thirds between 400 and 600). For the sample items, the report includes item-level information such as difficulty in score points and the percentage of students answering correctly across OECD countries when available. Because this is a question-and-scoring compilation rather than an empirical modeling study, it does not estimate effects, train ML models, or report PV/missing-data handling for an analysis pipeline.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a non-empirical OECD report that compiles publicly available PISA sample questions and scoring guidance, rather than conducting an original student-level analysis. Consequently, there is no dependent variable modeled, no ML algorithm evaluated, and no analytic sample with weights, PVs, or missing-data procedures. The presence of country lists and item-level correctness percentages reflects descriptive reporting for illustrative purposes, not a statistical estimation framework.
